lessons.title: Ticket Size and Financing: Home Loans vs Lease Rental Discounting

children.text: Walk into any bank branch with a salary slip and a flat you want to buy, and a home loan can be sanctioned within days at one of the lowest rates in Indian lending. Walk in wanting to buy a ₹3 crore office unit, and the conversation changes: smaller loan, higher rate, more documents, and questions about the tenant. The same bank treats a flat and an office as completely different risks. How each is financed changes the return you actually earn, often more than the yield itself.

body.text: A home loan lends against your salary. Lease rental discounting lends against your tenant's rent. Borrowing only helps your return when the property earns more than the loan costs.

children.text: Home Loans: Cheap Money Tied to Your Income

Home loans are the cheapest long-term borrowing most Indians can get. With the RBI repo rate at 5.25% in 2026, leading banks advertise home loan rates starting a little above 7%, with most borrowers paying somewhere between about 7.25% and 8.5% depending on credit score and loan size. Tenures run up to 30 years.

markDefs.definition: Fixed Obligation to Income Ratio: the share of your monthly income already committed to EMIs. Banks typically want total EMIs, including the new loan, to stay within about 50% to 60% of income.
The loan amount as a percentage of the property's value. A lower LTV means a larger down payment from the buyer.

children.text: The bank's real security is your income, not the rent. Lenders check your
FOIR
to make sure you can pay the EMI even if the flat never earns a rupee. The RBI also caps the
loan-to-value (LTV) ratio
on housing loans.
Financing Commercial Property

markDefs.definition: A loan in which a bank lends against the future rent a leased commercial property will earn over the remaining lease, with the rent routed through an escrow account to repay the loan.

children.text: Banks see commercial property as a business asset. Buying an unleased office or shop usually means a commercial property purchase loan or a loan against property, with a lower LTV, often around 50% to 65% of value, shorter tenures and higher rates. Once the property has a tenant, a far better tool opens up:
lease rental discounting (LRD)

In LRD, the bank calculates the present value of the rent still due under the lease, and lends a share of it, typically around 70% to 80% of that discounted value, subject to a cap based on the property's market value. The loan tenure usually matches the remaining lease, often 7 to 15 years. Rates are generally higher than home loans.

body.label: How LRD repayment works
body.value: Rent goes to an escrow account first
body.context: The tenant pays rent into an escrow account controlled by the bank. The bank takes the EMI, then releases the balance to the owner. Your EMI is paid by the tenant, not your salary.

body.caption: n is the months left on the lease and r is the monthly discount rate. Banks also cap the loan at a share of the property's market value.

body.title: Worked example: LRD on a Mumbai office unit

children.text: An office unit worth ₹4.5 crore earns ₹3 lakh a month, with 7 years (84 months) left on the lease. The bank discounts the rent at 9.5% a year and lends 75% of the present value.

Present value of 84 monthly payments of ₹3 lakh at 9.5%: about ₹1.84 crore. Loan at 75%: about ₹1.38 crore. The value cap of 65% of ₹4.5 crore is ₹2.93 crore, so the rent-based figure of ₹1.38 crore applies.

The EMI on ₹1.38 crore at 9.5% over 84 months works out to ₹2.25 lakh, exactly 75% of the rent. That is no coincidence. Lending 75% of rent discounted at the loan rate produces an EMI equal to 75% of rent. The tenant's rent repays the loan, and the owner keeps ₹75,000 a month.

body.text: LRD depends on the lease surviving. If the tenant leaves after its lock-in, the rent stops flowing into escrow but the EMI does not. Banks may then ask you to pay from your own pocket, prepay part of the loan, or find a new tenant quickly. Check that the lock-in covers a meaningful part of the loan tenure before you borrow.

children.text: When Borrowing Helps and When It Hurts

markDefs.definition: Positive leverage: when a property's yield is higher than the interest rate on the loan, so borrowing increases the income return on your own money. Negative leverage is the reverse.

children.text: Leverage is
positive

when the property earns a higher yield than the loan costs, and negative when it earns less. Compare the income return on your own money in two simple cases, using interest only and ignoring principal repayment and transaction costs.

body.caption: Income return on your own money, before appreciation

body.title: Income return on own money, with and without a loan (%)

children.text: Both cases show negative leverage on income, because both yields are below their loan rates. But the scale is completely different. The flat's rent does not even cover the interest, so the owner tops up ₹3.72 lakh a year and depends entirely on appreciation. The office still produces positive cash after interest. Its return on equity dips from 8% to 6.5%, but the rent services the debt.

body.text: Leverage magnifies appreciation in both cases, which is why people borrow. But only commercial property, at typical Indian yields, can usually carry its own loan. With residential, your salary carries the loan while you wait for prices to rise.

body.title: Quick Check: The RBI LTV Cap
body.question: Ananya wants to buy a ₹1 crore flat in Pune with a home loan. Under the RBI's LTV caps, what is the maximum loan she can get against the property value?
body.explanation: For housing loans above ₹75 lakh, the RBI caps LTV at 75%, so the maximum is ₹75 lakh. Ananya needs at least ₹25 lakh of her own money, plus stamp duty and registration.

body.title: Calculate: LRD Loan on a Chennai Office
body.prompt: A leased office on OMR, Chennai earns ₹2.5 lakh a month with 96 months left on the lease. The present value of that rent, discounted at 10% a year, is about ₹164.75 lakh. The bank lends 70% of the present value. How much can the owner borrow, in ₹ lakh? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: 70% × ₹164.75 lakh = ₹115.3 lakh, or about ₹1.15 crore, provided this is within the bank's cap based on the property's market value.

body.title: Scenario: Two Flats or One Pre-Leased Unit?
body.scenario: Karan, a 45-year-old business owner in Ahmedabad, has ₹1.5 crore of his own money. Option A: buy two flats worth ₹1.5 crore each in Mumbai using home loans, needing about ₹75 lakh of equity each, and rent them out at a combined ₹70,000 a month. Option B: buy one ₹3 crore pre-leased office in GIFT City, Gandhinagar, yielding 8% net, funded with ₹1.5 crore of his own money and ₹1.5 crore of LRD at 9.5%. His business income is seasonal.
body.prompt: Compare the monthly cash flow of each option and advise him.
body.modelAnswer: Option A: two home loans of ₹1.125 crore each, ₹2.25 crore in total, at around 8% over 20 years mean EMIs of roughly ₹1.88 lakh a month against ₹70,000 of rent, before maintenance and property tax. Karan would fund about ₹1.18 lakh a month from seasonal business income, which is dangerous. Option B: net income of ₹24 lakh a year, ₹2 lakh a month, against interest of about ₹1.19 lakh a month on the LRD, and the escrow structure pays the loan from rent. Even after principal repayment, the tenant largely services the loan. Option B suits a seasonal income far better, provided the tenant is strong and the lock-in covers much of the loan tenure. Option A is a bet on Mumbai appreciation funded by his salary. If he chooses B, he should verify the tenant's strength and keep a cash reserve in case the tenant leaves.

cards.definition: Loan amount as a percentage of property value; RBI caps it at 90%, 80% or 75% for housing loans depending on size.
Fixed Obligation to Income Ratio: share of income committed to EMIs, used to size home loans.
A loan against the present value of future rent from a leased commercial property.
An account controlled by the lender where rent is deposited and the EMI deducted before the balance reaches the owner.
When a property's yield exceeds the loan rate, so borrowing boosts the income return on equity.
When a property's yield is below the loan rate, so borrowing reduces the income return on equity.

points: Residential entry tickets are smaller and financed by cheap home loans; commercial property needs bigger cheques and costlier, lower-LTV finance.
RBI caps housing loan LTV at 90% up to ₹30 lakh, 80% up to ₹75 lakh and 75% above that.
Home loans are sized on your income; LRD is sized on the present value of your tenant's remaining rent.
In LRD, rent flows through escrow to pay the EMI, but the loan remains your obligation if the tenant leaves.
Leverage only helps income returns when yield exceeds the loan rate; Indian residential yields are far below home loan rates.
Pre-leased commercial property can usually carry its own debt, while residential debt is carried by your salary.

body.text: Interest rates, LTV limits, LRD terms and loan amounts vary by lender, borrower profile and time. Rates referenced are indicative for 2026. Examples simplify loan structures and ignore fees and taxes. This lesson is educational and is not a recommendation to borrow or to buy any property.
